summary: Defines SNMP management objects for IEEE 802.3 Medium Attachment Units, the parts that connect Ethernet devices to cables. It replaced RFC 2239 and was replaced by RFC 3636.

plainLanguage.summary: Readouts for the plug-in part that links a computer to the wire, showing its type and condition.

subtitle: SNMP objects for managing the Ethernet MAUs that connect devices to the cable, now including 1000 Mb/s.

tldr.problem: Network managers need a standard way to read and configure the Medium Attachment Units that attach Ethernet repeaters and interfaces to the medium, including newer 1000 Mb/s types.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a MIB module (MAU-MIB) based on IEEE Std 802.3, 1998 edition, with tables for repeater MAUs, interface MAUs, auto-negotiation, broadband MAUs and jack types, plus two jabber notifications.
tldr.outcome: It extends RFC 2239 with 1000 Mb/s, PAUSE negotiation and remote fault objects. It has since been obsoleted by RFC 3636.

today: RFC 2668 is a Proposed Standard that obsoleted RFC 2239, and it has itself been obsoleted by RFC 3636, which carries the MAU MIB forward.

sections.title: What the MAU MIB Covers
sections.content:
RFC 2668 defines part of the SNMP Management Information Base for IEEE 802.3 Medium Attachment Units (MAUs). It extends RFC 2239 and obsoletes it. It is intended as a superset of that MIB, which was to go to historic status.

The new objects add management of 1000 Mb/s devices, PAUSE negotiation and remote fault status. RFC 2239 had in turn replaced RFC 1515 and had added 100 Mb/s devices, auto-negotiation on interface MAUs and jack management.
sections.plainLanguage: The older list of gauges only knew about slower plugs. This newer list adds the very fast kind.

sections.title: Repeater MAUs and Interface MAUs
sections.content:
The definitions follow Section 30.5 and Annex 30A of IEEE Std 802.3, 1998 edition. For convenience the RFC calls the devices "repeater MAUs" (attached to 802.3 repeaters) and "interface MAUs" (attached to Ethernet-like interfaces).

Interface MAU objects extend the Interfaces MIB. An agent implementing them MUST also implement the relevant Interfaces MIB groups, and ifMauIfIndex equals the ifIndex of the interface the MAU is connected to. Repeater MAU objects extend the 802.3 Repeater MIB, which an agent implementing them MUST also implement. Internal MAUs, whose functions live entirely inside a device, may be managed under dot3RpMauBasicGroup or dot3IfMauBasicGroup.
sections.plainLanguage: Some plugs belong to a hub that shares the wire among many computers, and some belong to a single computer. Each kind has its own set of gauges.

sections.title: The MAU-MIB Module
sections.content:
The module sits under snmpDot3MauMgt, which is { mib-2 26 }. It is written in SMIv2 and defines object groups for repeater MAUs (rpMauTable), interface MAUs (ifMauTable), auto-negotiation (ifMauAutoNegTable) and broadband MAUs (broadMauBasicTable).

Typical objects report a MAU's type, status, whether media is available, the jabber state and a count of false carriers. A JackType convention lists connectors such as rj45(2), bnc(5) and fiberSC(8). A list of dot3MauType identities names MAU types such as dot3MauType10BaseT and 1000BASE variants, with half and full duplex versions.
sections.plainLanguage: For each plug, the list says what type it is, whether a cable is attached and whether it is behaving badly.

sections.title: Auto-Negotiation and Notifications
sections.content:
The auto-negotiation table covers interface MAUs. Objects include ifMauAutoNegAdminStatus, the capabilities a MAU has, advertises and receives from its partner, a restart object and remote fault objects. Setting ifMauAutoNegRestart can restart negotiation.

Two notifications are defined, rpMauJabberTrap for repeater MAUs and ifMauJabberTrap for interface MAUs, to report a jabber condition.
sections.plainLanguage: Two plugs can talk to each other about the best speed they both can use, and these controls let a manager watch and restart that chat.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Several objects are read-write, and setting them can seriously affect the network. Examples named are enabling or disabling a MAU, changing its default type, enabling, disabling or restarting auto-negotiation, and changing the capabilities advertised during auto-negotiation. SNMPv1 alone is an insecure environment for such SET operations.

The RFC recommends that implementers consider SNMPv3, specifically the User-based Security Model (RFC 2574) and the View-based Access Control Model (RFC 2575).
sections.plainLanguage: Some of the switches change how the network works, so only trusted people should be able to flip them.
